questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the sectional compromises of the 1850s failed
questions.stem: Your structural brief for a state capitol restoration must explain why the sequence of compromises from 1820 through 1854 broke down instead of settling the question of slavery.

answer.exemplar: Each compromise bought time by postponing the question rather than resolving it. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 drew a line that did not cover later purchases of land. The Compromise of 1850 allowed slavery in the new territories by popular sovereignty, which meant the vote would decide before the question was settled. The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 repealed that arrangement and produced violence in Kansas, and the Dred Scott decision of 1857 removed the last constitutional means of restricting slavery in the territories. Each step narrowed the space for agreement rather than widening it.

questions.explanation: Every compromise postponed the question instead of settling it, and each later measure narrowed the options still further. By 1857 no lawful mechanism remained to limit slavery's spread.
questions.hint: Ask what each compromise deferred rather than decided.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the constitutional gap the Dred Scott ruling created

stimulus.body: That the preamble to the Constitution declares that all men are created equal does not apply to persons held as slaves, since it was not the intent of the framers to include them. The rights of property in slaves, and the right of the owner to the service of the slave, are recognized by the Constitution as existing and protected by it.

questions.stem: The heritage statement in your brief for a memorial hall must explain what gap this opinion created and what constitutional response it made necessary.

options.text: It denied national citizenship to Black Americans, requiring an amendment to grant it expressly

options.misconception: Mistakes the ruling for a trade measure

options.text: It barred states from taxing inheritances, requiring an amendment to restore revenue powers
options.misconception: Invents a tax holding in the opinion

options.text: It voided the Kansas constitution, requiring an amendment to validate state governments
options.misconception: Attaches a Kansas holding to the opinion

questions.explanation: By holding that Black Americans could not be citizens, the ruling left citizenship unsettled and made an amendment necessary to state it in the Constitution. Nothing about the trade or taxation appears in the holding.
questions.hint: Ask who was excluded and what a statute could not fix.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how sharecropping shaped the post-emancipation rural economy
questions.stem: The programme narrative for a restored farmstead must explain how the arrangement that replaced slavery kept freedpeople's families in economic dependence.

answer.exemplar: Sharecropping and tenancy replaced slavery as the dominant arrangement on southern farms. Families who worked land owned by others received a share of the crop and credit advances, but the landlord held the title, supplied the tools and animals, and kept the accounts. Because the crop had to be divided before debts were settled, a bad year or an dishonest count left the tenant owing money and dependent on the landlord's credit. The arrangement spread across the cotton belt and shaped Black rural life for generations after federal Reconstruction ended.

questions.explanation: Tenants received a share of a crop on land they did not own and owed accounts to the landlord, who controlled credit and the books. That structure reproduced dependence without legal bondage.
questions.hint: Follow who held the title and who kept the accounts.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Fourteenth Amendment was needed after the war
questions.stem: Preparing the brief for a reconstructed courthouse, you must explain why a war victory and the Thirteenth Amendment were not enough to protect freedpeople's rights.

answer.exemplar: Ending slavery as a legal status did not define who was a citizen or what states owed the people within their borders. The Fourteenth Amendment supplied both. It established citizenship at birth as a national right, so no state could deny a person citizenship on the ground of state birth, and it prohibited state laws that abridge the privileges of citizens, deny equal protection, or deprive life, liberty, or property without due process. It also barred states from escaping the war's cost by refusing to pay debts incurred for it.

questions.explanation: Abolition left the status of citizenship and the reach of state law unresolved, and a court ruling had recently made both dangerous. The amendment filled that gap and attached readmission to it.
questions.hint: Ask what remained undefined after the Thirteenth Amendment.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the Missouri Compromise depended on a constitutional reading
questions.stem: Before your first client meeting on a statehouse restoration, you must explain why the 1820 bargain rested on a particular constitutional interpretation.

answer.exemplar: The bargain rested on the reading that Congress could set the terms of state admission and so limit slavery in the territories, while a prohibition on a territorial line did not touch property rights already secured to citizens. Southerners accepted it only on the promise that the restriction would not apply to territory they might acquire later. That proviso, tied to the wording of the Louisiana Purchase, became the crack through which the whole settlement later broke.

questions.explanation: Congress could set the terms of state admission, so it could limit slavery in territories, and the deal was sold as protecting existing property. Its wording covered only the 1803 purchase, and that limit is where it later broke.
questions.hint: The text's wording, not just its spirit, matters here.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the end of Reconstruction produced long disenfranchisement
questions.stem: Explaining the sequence of interpretive panels for a state museum, you must explain how the legal framework established in 1868 and 1870 came to be enforced in only a few southern states.

answer.exemplar: The constitutional guarantees of the Fourteenth and Fifteenth Amendments survived the end of Reconstruction, but enforcement did not. After federal troops left the South in 1877, most state governments amended their constitutions to add literacy tests, understanding clauses, registration hurdles, and poll taxes, and courts gave those measures a broad reading. Black citizens who had voted for a decade found the franchise closing within a few years. Enforcement would not return in force until the civil rights acts and court decisions of the middle twentieth century.

questions.explanation: Once federal troops and federal elections were gone, state constitutions and state courts rewrote the rules of voting. The constitutional text stayed; the enforcement mechanism disappeared.
questions.hint: Ask what happened to the rules once the troops left.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the election of 1860 became the justification for secession
questions.stem: In your competition entry, you must explain the step by which a lawful election became the legal justification for seven states leaving the Union.

answer.exemplar: Lincoln's election was the trigger, and the argument was framed as a question of law. The Republican candidate had pledged not to end slavery where it existed, but Southern leaders read his victory as a sectional mandate, and legislators debated whether the president would have the power to interfere with slavery in the states. Seven Deep South states then acted on the claim that secession was a lawful remedy for an unconstitutional condition, while four upper South states waited. The election created no legal crisis; the crisis came from reading the result as a threat to property.

questions.explanation: Lincoln's lawful victory was interpreted as a threat to slavery, and secession was framed as a constitutional right rather than an act of rebellion. The legal argument, not any act of violence, produced the break.
questions.hint: The election was legal; the reading of it was not.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Battle of Gettysburg is treated as a turning point
questions.stem: Writing the gallery text for your war museum's central hall, you must explain why a single battle in Pennsylvania carried such weight.

answer.exemplar: Gettysburg mattered for three connected reasons. It ended Robert Lee's second and last invasion of the north at the moment when the Confederacy's best field army was at its strongest. It inflicted casualties the Confederacy could not replace from a shrinking pool of white soldiers, while the Union could and did bring in far more men. It also gave the Union a single dramatic occasion on which to dedicate a cemetery and speak of the war's meaning, which made the emancipation of enslaved people in rebel areas a stated war aim rather than a wartime expedient.

questions.explanation: The battle ended the Confederacy's best offensive, inflicted losses it could not replace, and gave the Union a moment to define the war's purpose through emancipation. Together they made 1863 decisive.
questions.hint: Ask what Lee's army could not afford to keep losing.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the Kansas-Nebraska Act ended the sectional bargain
questions.stem: Preparing a talk for your firm's heritage seminar, you must explain why a statute about western territories is usually described as the moment the sectional bargain broke.

answer.exemplar: The Kansas-Nebraska Act of 1854 did three things at once. It opened roughly half a million square miles of territory to settlement, which Southerners wanted for the possibility of a slave state and Northerners wanted for free statehood. It repealed the Missouri Compromise and the Compromise of 1850 territorial arrangements, replacing them with popular sovereignty, which meant the question would be decided by who voted first. And it triggered a rush of fraudulent elections, rival governments, and violence in Kansas, which showed that no agreement could be trusted to hold without federal force.

questions.explanation: The act repealed earlier bargains, opened the question to a popular vote, and produced violence that made every later agreement look unenforceable to one side or the other. It made honest compromise seem impossible.
questions.hint: Ask what the act repealed and what it set in its place.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how sharecropping differed from slavery as a labour arrangement
questions.stem: In the curatorial plan for a farmhouse exhibit you must explain the differences between the old system and the new one without denying how much resembled the old.

answer.exemplar: Sharecropping differed from slavery in form while resembling it in practice. There was no legal title in a person, no sale of the worker, and no ownership of children, and wage labour existed alongside crop sharing in some districts. But the landlord still controlled the land, the credit, and the inputs, and the tenant still had no independent way to support a household. The arrangement was therefore called free labour, and the freedpeople's own communities were divided over whether to accept it, with many elders arguing that it reproduced the old dependence.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the Fourteenth Amendment shifted the burden of justification
questions.stem: The public history section of your brief must explain why the amendment required states to give reasons for their laws.

answer.exemplar: The Fourteenth Amendment put the burden of justification on the government rather than on the person claiming a right. Equal protection and due process did not merely forbid certain laws; they required the state to show a sufficient reason for the laws it did pass. That structure is what made claims of unequal treatment justiciable in court rather than a matter of local politics, and it is why the amendment became the foundation for later campaigns against segregation and unequal voting rules. It applied to states, whose actions had previously been largely beyond federal reach.

questions.explanation: The amendment made government justify its laws to the people it governed, rather than leaving the burden on those claiming rights. That shift is what made rights enforceable in court against states.
questions.hint: Ask who has to explain themselves now, and to whom.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the arguments made for and against the Missouri Compromise
questions.stem: In the master plan for a statehouse restoration you must summarise the case for the 1820 arrangement and the case against it in the same paragraph.

answer.exemplar: Supporters argued that the arrangement preserved the Union, balanced the Senate, and honoured the Missouri constitution and the property rights already secured under the federal compact, while permanently closing the question of slavery in the remaining public lands. Critics answered that the act violated the Constitution's ban on slavery beyond the original states, that it made property rather than the national interest the measure of membership, and that the Missouri legislature had been admitted on terms the voters of the state had never been asked to accept. The compact satisfied both sections for a generation and neither for long.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how the compromise of 1877 affected federal enforcement
questions.stem: Advising on the exhibition's final display case, you must explain what changed once federal troops were withdrawn from the southern states.

questions.learningObjective: Explain the constitutional framing of the secession crisis
questions.stem: Summarizing the historical case in your competition entry, you must explain why southern leaders claimed a right to secede and why northern leaders rejected the claim.

answer.exemplar: Secessionists argued that the United States was a compact of states, and that a state might withdraw when the bargain was broken. questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of Black military service in 1863
questions.stem: Preparing a lecture on the war's decisive year, you must explain why the enrolment of Black men changed the arithmetic of the conflict.

answer.exemplar: Enlistment gave the Union a source of manpower it could not otherwise have found quickly, because the northern states had limited population and the war was consuming men faster than the states could supply them. questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a freedman's letter as a judgment on the new labour system

stimulus.body: I have now been on this place three years and the land is not mine, nor will it be while I owe a dollar of the account. I would rather have the wage I am paid here and the chance to save something in the winter, and I have concluded that the old master is no worse than the new landlord.

questions.stem: Consulting the payroll ledgers in your project archive, you must explain what this letter reveals about how former slaves judged their new position.

options.text: That freedpeople compared old and new masters pragmatically rather than defending the old system
That the writer regarded the old plantation system as superior in every respect
options.misconception: Presents the writer as preferring slavery

options.text: That the writer had secured clear ownership of the land he worked after three years
options.misconception: Claims the writer owned his land

options.text: That the writer had left agricultural labour entirely for wage work elsewhere
options.misconception: Claims the writer abandoned farm labour

questions.explanation: The writer measures the new arrangement against the old by what it pays and what it permits, finding the difference small without defending the old system. That pragmatism shaped how freedpeople approached sharecropping.
questions.hint: Notice what the writer compares and what they do not praise.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize how the Missouri Compromise shaped later constitutional interpretation
questions.stem: Evaluating the historical panel for your final gallery, you must show how a compromise of 1820 shaped the arguments of 1857 and beyond.

options.text: Its line became the reference point for later disputes over congressional power and the rights of citizens
Its wording was treated by the courts as a settled rule and never questioned again
options.misconception: Claims the act was never challenged

options.text: It was incorporated into the Constitution as a permanent clause in the amendment of 1868
options.misconception: Invents an 1868 incorporation of the act

options.text: It created the practice of counting each state equally in the Senate for all future debates
options.misconception: Attributes the equal rule to the 1820 act

questions.explanation: Because the act fixed a line and a supermajority rule for changing it, later disputes about congressional power returned to that wording, and the Dred Scott court read it restrictively. It framed the arguments that undid it.
questions.hint: Follow the line from 1820 to the court of 1857.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Identify the trigger that turned sectional tension into armed conflict
questions.stem: Before signing off on the elevations, you must identify the specific event that moved the dispute from the conference table to the battlefield.

options.text: The federal assault on the garrison at Fort Sumter in April 1861
The Supreme Court's ruling on the Missouri Compromise in 1857
options.misconception: Places the court ruling at the battlefield

options.text: The ratification of the Kansas constitution under the Lecompton settlement
options.misconception: Picks a Kansas event as the trigger

options.text: The withdrawal of the federal garrison from Fort Sumter in December 1860
options.misconception: Confuses the withdrawal with the assault

questions.explanation: The bombardment of the federal garrison in April 1861 was the first exchange of gunfire, the point where organised resistance became war. The earlier withdrawal of the garrison had been a last attempt to avoid it.
questions.hint: Look for the first use of force, not the last attempt at peace.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the role of the Northwest Ordinance in the slavery controversy
questions.stem: Writing the rationale for your exhibition's orientation gallery, you must explain why a law from 1787 kept returning to the argument about slavery.

answer.exemplar: The Northwest Ordinance of 1787 barred slavery in the territory north of the Ohio River, and it became a precedent that northerners could cite for the claim that Congress had the power to exclude slavery from new lands. Southerners accepted it as a concession already made for one territory but argued that it established no general principle, since the framers had provided for slavery in the territory south of the Ohio. The ordinance therefore anchored both sides of the later argument, and the Missouri Compromise was drafted with the memory of it in view.

questions.explanation: The ordinance showed that Congress could exclude slavery from a territory, which gave later acts their precedent, while southerners read it as a one-off bargain. It framed the Missouri debate of 1820.
questions.hint: Ask what the 1787 act proved about congressional power.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Explain what freedpeople demanded after the war and what they protected

stimulus.body: We, the undersigned laborers of the county, do respectfully ask the legislature of this state to place the property of the master in the hands of the freedmen who have tilled it, and to provide for the education of their children, and to protect them in the exercise of the rights the war has won for them, lest that the fruits of the sacrifice shall be taken away from us.

questions.stem: Consulting the committee report that accompanies your project archive, you must explain what the petitioners took from the war's outcome and what they wanted in its place.

options.text: That emancipation and citizenship should be made permanent in law and not left to local discretion
That the war's debts should be cancelled so that no tax burden would fall on their county
options.misconception: Misreads the petition as a demand for debt relief

options.text: That the state legislature should abolish all property titles in the counties that rebelled
options.misconception: Turns the request into a general confiscation

options.text: That military courts should remain in charge of the counties for a further ten years
options.misconception: Invents a demand to extend military rule

questions.explanation: The petitioners treat emancipation and the rights won by the war as a national settlement that state governments should not undo, which is the demand the Fourteenth Amendment answered. They ask for law, not charity.
questions.hint: Note the phrase about something being won and then undone.

questions.subject: US_HISTORY
questions.learningObjective: Synthesize why the end of Reconstruction is still debated as cause or consequence
questions.stem: Concluding the interpretive account in your gallery, you must set out the two readings of 1877 that historians still defend against each other.

options.text: Whether the retreat caused the long disenfranchisement, or whether that outcome was already inevitable
Whether the amendments were legally valid, a question still formally unsettled in court
options.misconception: Presents validity as still unadjudicated

options.text: Whether federal troops should have remained in the South permanently under the plan
options.misconception: Turns the debate into a policy argument about troop levels

options.text: Whether the southern states had been legally readmitted at all, since no instrument exists
options.misconception: Claims their readmission was never valid

questions.explanation: Historians divide over whether the withdrawal of troops ended a working order and caused the disenfranchisement, or whether southern determination had already made the outcome inevitable.
questions.hint: Ask whether 1877 caused the change or confirmed it.
